claims.text: Across all 29 countries, problematic social media users reported lower life satisfaction than non-problematic users.
Across all 29 countries, problematic social media users reported more psychological complaints than non-problematic users.
Across all 29 countries, problematic social media users reported lower school satisfaction than non-problematic users.
Across all 29 countries, problematic social media users reported higher perceived school pressure than non-problematic users.
Across all 29 countries, problematic social media users reported lower family support than non-problematic users.
Across all 29 countries, problematic social media users reported lower friend support than non-problematic users.
In countries with a higher prevalence of intense social media use, intense users reported higher life satisfaction and family support than non-intense users.
In countries with a lower prevalence of intense social media use, intense users reported lower life satisfaction, lower family support, and more psychological complaints than non-intense users.
In all 29 countries, intense social media users reported higher levels of friend support than non-intense users.
Country-level prevalence rates of intense and problematic social media use were not significantly associated with mobile broadband costs or internet speed.

evidence.description: Problematic SMU was negatively associated with life satisfaction across countries (B = -0.823, p < .001; 95% PI = -1.179 to -0.467).
Problematic SMU was positively associated with psychological complaints across countries (B = 0.619, p < .001; 95% PI = 0.396 to 0.842).
Problematic users reported lower school satisfaction (B = -0.316, p < .001; 95% PI = -0.480 to -0.152).
Problematic users reported higher school pressure (B = 0.292, p < .001; 95% PI = 0.077 to 0.507).
Problematic users reported less family support than nonproblematic users across all countries (B = -0.619, p < .001; 95% PI = -0.826 to -0.396).
Problematic users reported lower levels of friend support across all countries (B = -0.343, p < .001; 95% PI = -0.516 to -0.144).
Cross-level interaction between intense SMU and country-level intense SMU prevalence was positive for life satisfaction (B = 1.229, p < .001) and family support (B = 0.816, p < .001).

Cross-level interaction showed intense users reported lower life satisfaction and family support and more psychological complaints (B = -0.533, p = .002) in countries with lower intense SMU prevalence.
In all countries, intense users reported higher levels of friend support than nonintense users (B = 0.327, p < .001; 95% PI = 0.115 to 0.545).

Mobile broadband costs and internet speed did not explain differences in country-level prevalence of intense SMU (B = 0.000, p = .628; B = -0.005, p = .254) or problematic SMU (B = 0.000, p = .568; B = -0.001, p = .338).

methodologies.name: Two-level hierarchical regression modeling
methodologies.description: Conducted two-level regression analyses on cross-national survey data with individual-level measures at level 1 and country-level measures at level 2, testing random slopes and cross-level interactions.
datasets: 2017/2018 Health Behaviour in School-aged Children (HBSC) survey
conditions: Control for gender, age, and family affluence

limitations.text: Mental, school, and social well-being were measured using either single or a few items, which may have limited the representation of well-being constructs.
The cross-sectional design of the study does not allow for causal inferences regarding the relationship between social media use and well-being.
All measures were based on self-reports, which may deviate from actual time spent on social media.
The measure of intense social media use captured active communicative use rather than passive scrolling.
Existing research on intense and problematic social media use typically relies on single-country data, limiting cross-national generalizability.
Prior studies typically failed to examine intense and problematic social media use simultaneously in a single analytical model.

future_work.text: Replicate findings using more detailed and multi-item measures of well-being.
Conduct longitudinal research to establish the direction of causality between social media use and well-being.
Use objective measures of social media use, such as smartphone application tracking apps.
